TextView.android:text: Set up in order. Each step unlocks the next.
The pad and its panel are windows drawn over whatever is on the second screen. Android asks you to allow this once.
SidePad runs in the background with a notification. Allowing it gives you Show, Edit and Stop buttons there. The pad works without it.
The first start opens a short guide on the second screen. Everything else lives there: pull down from its top edge for the SidePad panel, pull up from its bottom edge to show or hide the pad.

Switch.android:text: Start in the background at boot
Floating button to show and hide the pad

TextView.android:text: For a handheld with one screen, where every edge swipe belongs to Android and there is no spare gesture to reach the pad with. Drag the button anywhere; tap it to show or hide the pad, hold it to open the panel.

Switch.android:text: Forget the machine when it disconnects

TextView.android:text: On a Mac a pairing survives a disconnection but the controller does not — macOS files a handheld as a phone and takes the phone route back, which carries no gamepad. The pairing then looks fine and the pad does nothing. This throws our side away as the link drops, so both ends agree it is gone and the next session starts from a fresh pairing, which always works. You still have to forget it on the machine itself; no controller can make a host forget. Leave this off for machines where reconnecting does work.
Only needed if a button does nothing when the pad is forwarding to another machine. Some handhelds put Start and Select on a separate input device, which the pad cannot find on its own.

For a game that does not recognise the pad and numbers its buttons in order instead. Leave this off first: if the face buttons come out shifted — R1 acting as Start, Y acting as a shoulder, X doing nothing — turn it on. M1 and M2 are not sent in this order. The machine has to reconnect before it notices.

Switch.android:text: Tell a machine the pad can rumble

TextView.android:text: On, games can buzz the handheld. Off, the pad does not mention motors at all, for a machine that behaves badly when offered them. On a Mac this makes no difference to anything but the rumbling — it runs its haptics loop either way. The machine has to disconnect and reconnect before it notices the change.
Launchers that cache icons (Beacon, ES-DE, Daijishō) show the new one after they restart.

Your presets and the current layout live inside the app and are lost when it is uninstalled. Export writes them to a file you choose (Downloads, a cloud folder); Import reads such a file back, replacing presets of the same name.

Shizuku itself stops when the Thor reboots. In the Shizuku app, turn on “Start on boot (wireless debugging)” so both come back on their own; otherwise start Shizuku again from its app or from a computer with adb.
